items.stimulus: Mice raised in completely germ-free cages develop severe allergic reactions to harmless pollen far more often than mice raised in ordinary cages. Because the two groups of mice differ only in their contact with microbes, immunologist Rhea Kandel and her team hypothesize that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: early contact with microbes helps the immune system learn to tolerate harmless substances.
pollen carries harmful microbes that directly provoke allergic reactions in exposed mice.
mice in ordinary cages encounter more pollen overall than germ-free mice encounter.
all mice exposed to microbes early in life will remain free of allergies permanently.
items.explanation: The surprise is that the mice with no microbes have more allergies. The text says the only difference between the groups is contact with microbes, so the explanation has to involve microbes helping in some way. If early microbial contact teaches the immune system not to overreact, then the germ-free mice, which missed that contact, would overreact to pollen. That is exactly what the text reports.

B.why: This explanation sounds scientific, but it gets the direction wrong. If microbes caused the allergies, the germ-free mice would have fewer of them, not more. You fell into the subtype's trap by ignoring which group reacted.

C.why: The text says the groups differ only in their contact with microbes. A difference in pollen exposure is ruled out by that detail, so you skipped the comparison the passage sets up.

D.why: Look at 'all' and 'permanently.' The text shows only that allergies are less common in mice raised with microbes. That doesn't mean every such mouse stays allergy-free forever. This is strength creep.

taught coastal communities to make pottery in the hilltop village's style.

items.stimulus: In earlier studies, adults who ate a high-fiber breakfast felt full longer than adults who ate a low-fiber breakfast. Nutrition researcher Tomás Ibarra suspected that this effect comes only from fiber that thickens into a gel in the stomach. He therefore served high-fiber breakfasts made with fiber that does not thicken and anticipated that, compared with a low-fiber breakfast, these breakfasts would ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: keep participants feeling full for noticeably longer than the low-fiber breakfast.
make little or no difference in how long participants felt full afterward.
make participants feel hungry much sooner than the low-fiber breakfast did.
lead participants to eat larger portions of food at breakfast than usual.
items.explanation: Ibarra thinks the feeling of fullness comes only from fiber that thickens. His test breakfasts use fiber that doesn't thicken, which removes the cause he suspects. If he's right, the usual effect should disappear, so he would expect little or no difference from the low-fiber breakfast.

A.why: This is the original finding from earlier studies. Ibarra's setup takes away the ingredient he thinks causes it. You picked the original effect instead of the expected change, which is the subtype's trap.

D.why: The study measures how long participants feel full after eating. Portion size at breakfast is never discussed, so this choice answers a different question.

items.stimulus: Inspectors have long checked steel bridges by tapping beams with hammers and listening for a dull sound. However, this method reveals a crack only after it has grown large enough to change the sound a beam makes. prevent cracks from ever forming in the steel beams of older bridges.
reduce the amount of noise that passing traffic produces on bridges.
reveal cracks at an earlier stage than inspectors tapping beams can.
items.explanation: The text names the flaw in the old method: tapping finds a crack only after it has grown large. A new method is worth testing because it might fix that flaw. Sensors that record vibrations all the time could pick up a crack before it becomes big enough to change the sound.

items.stimulus: After a large earthquake, aftershocks typically become weaker and less frequent as time passes. Near one volcano, however, aftershocks grew more frequent several weeks after a strong quake, and the increase was confined to the ground directly above a known chamber of molten rock. Seismologists studying the volcano hypothesize that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the original earthquake was much stronger than seismologists first estimated.
movement of molten rock beneath the volcano was producing the added quakes.
aftershocks everywhere tend to grow more frequent in the weeks after a quake.
molten rock beneath every volcano will cause aftershocks to grow more frequent.
items.explanation: The surprise is that aftershocks increased when they would normally fade. The key detail is where the increase happened: only above the chamber of molten rock. An explanation tied to the molten rock accounts for both the timing and the location.

A.why: A stronger original quake might explain more aftershocks overall. It doesn't explain why the increase stayed above the chamber of molten rock. You fell into the subtype's trap by ignoring the setting.

D.why: The text describes one volcano. Words like 'every' and 'will' stretch that single case into a universal rule the passage can't support.

items.stimulus: Ornithologists noticed something odd about great tits living in a large city: their songs were higher in pitch than the songs of great tits in nearby forests. The researchers also measured the background sound in both places. Most city noise, such as the rumble of traffic, is low in pitch. The forests were quiet. The team hypothesizes that city birds sing higher because ______
items.stem: Which choice best completes the researchers' explanation?
choices: higher-pitched songs are easier to hear over the low rumble of traffic.
forest birds sing at a higher pitch than city birds do.
every bird species in the city has raised the pitch of its song.
city birds sing more at night, when the traffic is quietest.
items.explanation: The puzzle is the higher pitch in the city. The passage gives you one detail that explains it: city noise is low-pitched. A song pitched above that noise stands out from it, so this explanation uses both the observation and the measurement. You will use this same move on harder 'the team hypothesizes that' questions: find the detail the passage put there on purpose, and choose the answer that connects it to the puzzle.

D.why: This sounds like a scientific explanation, but it skips the key detail. The passage is about pitch and low-pitched noise, and it never mentions when the birds sing. This is the trap for this kind of question: an explanation that sounds sensible but ignores the clue.

items.stem: Which choice best completes the researchers' explanation?
choices: they dislike having to switch between day and night shifts.
the factory pays them less than other factories in the region.
the higher pay lets the factory require rotating night shifts.
no worker will ever accept rotating shifts, whatever the pay.
items.explanation: The passage opens with the popular view, that pay drives quitting, and then undercuts it: this factory pays the most and still loses the most workers. C.why: This links the two details, but it explains the factory's policy rather than why workers quit, which is the question the passage asks.

items.stimulus: Air usually gets colder as you climb a mountain, so the bottom of a valley is normally warmer than the slopes above it. On calm winter nights in one mountain valley, though, meteorologists found the opposite: the valley floor was several degrees colder than the slopes. Cold air is denser, and therefore heavier, than warm air. The meteorologists hypothesize that on calm nights, ______
items.stem: Which choice best completes the researchers' explanation?
choices: cold air sinks down the slopes and collects on the valley floor.
the air on the slopes is colder than the air on the valley floor.
the valley floor is colder than the slopes on every night of the year.
strong winds carry snow down from the slopes to the valley floor.
items.explanation: The usual pattern flips: the valley floor is colder, not warmer. The passage gives you the reason in its last fact. Cold air is heavy, so when there is no wind it slides downhill and pools at the bottom. This is the 'effect flips' version of a hypothesis question. Once the passage tells you the pattern reversed, your answer has to explain the reversal, not the usual pattern.

B.why: This is the usual pattern, which the passage says reversed on these nights. This is the trap for flipped-effect questions: choosing the original effect instead of its reverse.

C.why: The finding applies only to calm winter nights. 'Every night of the year' is strength creep that the passage does not support.

items.stimulus: Palms are sensitive to cold: today they grow only in places where the ground rarely or never freezes. Many people would therefore be surprised to learn that paleobotanists have found fossilized palm fronds in 50-million-year-old rocks on an island off the coast of Antarctica. That island is now covered in ice for most of the year. To explain why palm fossils appear in such an unlikely place, the researchers hypothesize that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: palms living in the distant past could survive in places that stayed frozen for most of the year.
the island had a warm climate with little or no frost during the time when the palms were growing there.
the island was already covered in ice for most of the year during the time when the palms were growing there.
palms first appeared on this island and only later spread from there to warmer regions on other continents.
items.explanation: Start with the surprise: palms need ground that rarely or never freezes, yet their fossils turn up on an island that is icy today. Only one explanation fits every detail. When the palms were alive, the island must have been warm enough for them, so its climate has changed since then. This is the basic move behind every 'the researchers hypothesize that' question. Find the detail that doesn't fit, then choose the explanation that makes all the stated facts agree, without adding any new ones.

A.why: You picked an explanation that sounds scientific but drops the key detail. The passage says palms grow only where the ground rarely or never freezes. Saying ancient palms could survive a frozen climate goes against that fact. It doesn't solve the puzzle.

C.why: You took the island's present-day condition and applied it to the past. If the island had been icy 50 million years ago, cold-sensitive palms could not have grown there. That makes the puzzle worse instead of explaining it. The direction has to be that the island was warm then and is icy now.

D.why: You went past what the passage says. Nothing in it tells you where palms first appeared or how they spread. This choice also doesn't explain the puzzle, because a palm that started on the island would still need a warm climate to grow there.

items.stimulus: Curators have long blamed the uneven fading of blue pigment in Edo-period woodblock prints on uneven exposure to light. Conservator Hana Ueda, however, found that in prints from the Kisaragi workshop, the blue near each sheet's edges is far more faded than the blue at the center, even in prints kept in dark storage and displayed only under uniform lighting. a heavier coating of starch sizing helps shield the blue pigment from whatever causes it to fade.

starch sizing speeds the fading of the blue pigment wherever it has been applied most heavily.

items.stimulus: Folklorists often assume that a tale is best preserved near the place where it began. Yet the story of the Drowned Ferryman, which is set on the Varna River and is thought to have originated there, survives in mountain villages some 300 kilometers away but not in the villages along the river itself. Parish records show that the mountain villages were founded in the 1700s by families who fled the river valley after a series of floods, and that the valley was later resettled by migrants from the coast. These facts suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the tale began in the mountain villages and was later adapted to fit a setting on the Varna River.
the coastal migrants brought their own version of the tale with them when they resettled the valley.
tales are generally best preserved in places that lie far from where they first emerged.
the families who fled the floods carried the tale away with them, leaving no one in the valley to tell it.
items.explanation: The puzzle is that a river tale survives far from the river but not beside it. The records explain it. The valley's original people, who presumably told the tale, moved to the mountains, and the people who replaced them came from the coast. If the tale traveled with the displaced families, it would turn up in the mountains and be missing from the resettled valley, which is exactly what the passage describes.

the drought around 1900 BCE was far less severe in the basin than the pollen records indicate.
sheep in the Harrow Basin needed more water and forage than researchers have usually assumed.

items.explanation: Normally drought shifts herds toward sheep, because cattle need more water and forage. Tell Omran went the other way. the Oregon panels received more ultraviolet light than the Arizona panels received over the test.
Arizona's stronger sunlight did more harm to the coating than constant swelling and shrinking did.
repeated wetting and drying will crack any roof coating faster than intense sunlight can.

items.stimulus: Standard models predict that raising a wage floor reduces employment, since some jobs stop being worth their cost to employers. Studying one statewide increase, economist Lena Ostrowski compared towns where a single firm hires most local workers with towns where many firms compete for staff. Employment dipped slightly in the competitive towns but rose in the single-firm towns, and nearly all the added workers there were longtime residents who had not been seeking work, not newcomers. Ostrowski hypothesizes that before the increase, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the dominant firms had offered too few openings to employ every resident who wanted a job
firms in both kinds of towns had paid workers less than their labor was worth to the firm
the dominant firms had kept pay low enough that many residents judged a job not worth taking
residents of the competitive towns had been willing to relocate to wherever pay was rising
items.explanation: The puzzle is that a higher wage floor raised employment, but only in single-firm towns, and the new workers were local residents who had not been looking for work. One explanation fits all three details. Where one firm dominates, it can set pay low because workers have nowhere else to go, and at that low pay some residents decide a job isn't worth taking. When the floor forces pay up, those residents start working. In competitive towns, competition had already pushed pay up, so the floor only raised costs, and employment dipped as the standard model predicts.

A.why: You saw that the new workers were people who hadn't been working, but you blamed a shortage of jobs instead of a shortage of willing workers. If the firms had too few openings, making each worker more expensive would lead them to cut jobs, not add them. This choice predicts employment falling in single-firm towns, which is the opposite of what the passage reports.

B.why: You spotted the underpayment explanation but applied it to every town. If firms in competitive towns had also been underpaying, the floor should have raised employment there too. Instead it dipped, so this choice ignores the comparison group, which is the key detail.

D.why: Migration would explain a rise in one place and a dip in another, but the passage says the added workers were longtime residents, not newcomers. This choice explains the pattern by assuming something the passage rules out.

items.stimulus: Most algae-eating reef fish feed in sunlit shallows, where algae grow fastest. Divers were therefore surprised to find juveniles of one such goby clustered on deep, dim ledges where algae are sparse, while adults stayed in the shallows. Juveniles on the ledges grew more slowly than juveniles kept in shallow pens that excluded predators, yet they outlived unprotected juveniles released on shallow reefs from which all adults had been removed. The team hypothesizes that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: adult gobies defend the shallow feeding areas and force the juveniles down to the ledges
for juveniles, the safety of the ledges outweighs the faster growth the shallows would allow
for juveniles, the faster growth the shallows allow outweighs the danger of feeding there
predators in the shallows will kill any juvenile goby that does not shelter on the ledges
items.explanation: The surprise is that juveniles live where food is poor. The two comparisons give both sides of a trade-off. Juveniles in the shallows grow faster when protected from predators, so the shallows offer better food. Unprotected juveniles in the shallows die sooner than juveniles on the ledges, even with no adults around, so the shallows are more dangerous. Juveniles choose the ledges anyway, so the hypothesis has to be that, for them, safety matters more than faster growth.

A.why: Competition with adults sounds scientific, but you ignored a key detail of the setup. The unprotected juveniles were released on reefs where all the adults had been removed, and they still did worse than juveniles on the ledges. Adults can't be what drives the pattern.

C.why: You identified the trade-off correctly but settled it in the wrong direction. If faster growth outweighed the danger, juveniles would gather in the shallows. The passage says they gather on the ledges, so this choice describes the opposite of what the gobies actually do.

D.why: You saw that predation drives the pattern, then made the claim stronger than the evidence allows. The passage says ledge juveniles outlived unprotected ones. It doesn't say every unsheltered juvenile dies. 'Any' and 'will' go beyond that evidence.

the number of circulating memory T cells in a forearm determines how fast it clears the pathogen.

items.stimulus: Permeable pavement reduces stormwater runoff by letting rain pass through its pores into a gravel base and then into the soil below. choices: the pavement's pores clog more quickly over clay soil than they do over sandy soil.
clogging of the pores has no effect on how much runoff permeable pavement prevents.

the clay sections fall short because water drains slowly from their gravel base into the soil.

items.stimulus: In many regions, small earthquakes become more frequent when groundwater rises, because water seeping into faults weakens the friction holding them in place. In the Varra Basin, however, small quakes peak each year in late summer, when groundwater is at its lowest. Unlike the faults in those other regions, the Varra Basin's faults lie directly beneath a thick aquifer, whose water adds weight that presses the two sides of each fault together. items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: water seeping into the Varra Basin's faults in late summer weakens the friction along them.
the aquifer's weight, when it is greatest, pushes the Varra Basin's faults past their limit.
the aquifer, lighter in late summer, presses less firmly on the faults and lets them slip.
faults dry out as groundwater falls, growing more brittle and more likely to fracture.
items.explanation: Here the usual effect is flipped: quakes peak when groundwater is lowest. The detail that sets the Varra Basin apart is that the aquifer's weight clamps its faults together. B.why: You correctly saw that weight matters but got the direction backward. The aquifer is heaviest when groundwater is high, yet quakes peak when it is low. More clamping weight resists slipping.
